nodes.label: The Ottoman Empire
nodes.full: Istanbul: conqueror of Yemen in 1538 for the Red Sea and the prestige of the pilgrimage, driven out in 1636, and back again after 1849 — a distant, loss-making, chronically rebellious frontier.
nodes.src: background — Hathaway, 'The Arab Lands under Ottoman Rule' (2008).

nodes.label: The world market
nodes.full: The European trading companies and the coffee-drinking public they served: the demand that made Mocha rich, and — once the plant was carried to Java and Brazil — the market that made it poor.
nodes.src: background — Tuchscherer, 'Le commerce du café' (2001).

nodes.label: The first Saudi state & Muhammad ʿAli
nodes.full: The Wahhabi Emirate raiding Asir and Najran from 1803, and the Egypt of Muhammad ʿAli that occupied the Tihama in the 1830s while fighting it — two outside forces that hollowed the imamate from the north.
nodes.src: background — Ibn Bishr; the Egyptian sources on Arabia.

nodes.label: Britain and British India
nodes.full: Bombay and London: the seizure of Aden in 1839, the treaty net over the hinterland, and the anti-slavery pressure on the Red Sea trade.
nodes.src: background — Gavin, 'Aden under British Rule 1839–1967' (1975).

nodes.label: The steamship and Suez
nodes.full: The technology that remade the Red Sea: the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 turned Aden into a top coaling port and raised Yemen's strategic value enough to bring the Ottomans back.
nodes.src: background — Gavin (1975); Headrick, 'The Tools of Empire' (1981).

nodes.label: The Ottoman conquest of Yemen
nodes.full: Suleiman Pasha's India-bound fleet seized Aden by treachery in 1538, and Ozdemir Pasha then fought his way up to take Sanaa by 1552. Yemen became an Ottoman eyalet — the empire's furthest and least governable Arab province.
nodes.src: al-Nahrawali, al-Barq al-Yamani fi'l-fath al-ʿUthmani; Clive Smith, 'Lahj and Aden'; Jane Hathaway, 'The Arab Lands under Ottoman Rule' (2008).

nodes.label: Garrison and revolt
nodes.full: The Ottomans held Yemen through a chain of garrison forts, a coffee-export monopoly at Mocha and heavy taxation — and faced near-continuous revolt, above all the great highland rising of 1567 that Sinan Pasha spent years suppressing.
nodes.src: al-Nahrawali; the Ottoman provincial records; Michel Tuchscherer on Ottoman Yemen and coffee.

nodes.label: Imam al-Qasim the Great and the war of expulsion
nodes.full: Al-Mansur al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, 'al-Qasim the Great', raised the Zaydi tribes against the Ottomans and founded the Qasimid line. He died before the job was done, but the tide had turned.
nodes.src: the Qasimid chronicles; Yahya ibn al-Husayn, Ghayat al-amani; R. B. Serjeant and R. Lewcock (eds), 'Sanʿaʾ: An Arabian Islamic City' (1983).

nodes.label: Imam al-Muʾayyad Muhammad completes the reconquest
nodes.full: Al-Qasim's son al-Muʾayyad Muhammad drove the last Ottoman forces out in 1635–36 and ruled a unified Yemen from Sanaa — the first native dynasty to hold the whole country since the Rasulids.
nodes.src: Yahya ibn al-Husayn, Ghayat al-amani; the Ottoman evacuation is dated 1635/36 in both the Yemeni and Ottoman sources.

nodes.label: Imam al-Mutawakkil Ismaʿil and the Qasimid apogee
nodes.full: Under al-Mutawakkil Ismaʿil the Qasimid state reached from Asir in the north to Hadramawt and Dhofar in the east — the largest Zaydi polity in history, floated on the customs revenue of the Mocha coffee monopoly.
nodes.src: Ghayat al-amani; Robert Wilson, 'Gazetteer of Historical North-West Yemen'; Tuchscherer on the coffee revenue.

nodes.label: The turn to hereditary succession
nodes.full: The imamate began passing within Bayt al-Qasim by inheritance rather than by the classic Zaydi 'rising' of a qualified claimant. That quietly gutted the theory of the office and left the dynasty open to challenge from other sayyid houses.
nodes.src: Bernard Haykel, 'Revival and Reform in Islam: The Legacy of Muhammad al-Shawkani' (2003); Gabriele vom Bruck on Sanʿaʾ sayyid families.

nodes.label: The peripheries break away
nodes.full: Lahej and Aden went to the ʿAbdali sultans after 1728, the Tihama to the Sharif of Abu Arish, Asir to its own emirs, and Hadramawt to the Kathiri and the rising Quʿayti. The Qasimid state shrank back to the highlands it had started from.
nodes.src: Clive Smith, 'Lahj and Aden'; R. B. Serjeant on the Hadramawt sultanates; Wilson's Gazetteer.

nodes.label: The Wahhabi and Egyptian incursions
nodes.full: The first Saudi state raided Asir and Najran from 1803; then Muhammad ʿAli of Egypt occupied the Tihama and Asir in the 1830s while fighting the Saudis. The imamate, already reduced, lost the coast entirely for a decade.
nodes.src: ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Rafiʿi and the Egyptian sources on Muhammad ʿAli in Arabia; Wilson's Gazetteer.

nodes.label: The East India Company takes Aden
nodes.full: After the plunder of a wrecked ship flying British colours, Commander Stafford Haines seized Aden from the ʿAbdali sultan of Lahej with a landing party. It became a possession of the Bombay Presidency and a free port.
nodes.src: Gordon Waterfield, 'Sultans of Aden' (1968); R. J. Gavin, 'Aden under British Rule 1839–1967' (1975).

nodes.label: Aden, Suez and the treaty hinterland
nodes.full: The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 made Aden one of the busiest coaling ports in the world and a cosmopolitan colonial city. To secure the water and the approaches, Britain signed a widening web of protection and stipend treaties with the hinterland shaykhs.
nodes.src: Gavin, 'Aden under British Rule' (1975); the Aden treaty series in Aitchison's 'Treaties, Engagements and Sanads'.

nodes.label: The Ottoman return
nodes.full: The Ottomans retook the Tihama and Hodeida in 1849 and, after Suez raised Yemen's strategic value, reoccupied Sanaa in 1872 under Ahmed Muhtar Pasha, creating the Vilayet of Yemen.
nodes.src: Caesar Farah, 'The Sultan's Yemen: Nineteenth-Century Challenges to Ottoman Rule' (2002); Thomas Kuehn, 'Empire, Islam, and Politics of Difference: Ottoman Rule in Yemen' (2011).

nodes.label: The Vilayet at war
nodes.full: Ottoman rule in the highlands meant permanent counter-insurgency against the Zaydi tribes and the Hamid al-Din imams, huge garrisons, recurrent famine, and a great rising in 1891–92. By 1900 the empire held the towns and the roads and little else.
nodes.src: Farah, 'The Sultan's Yemen' (2002); Kuehn (2011); the Ottoman Yemen army returns.

nodes.label: The great highland rising of 1567
nodes.full: A near-general revolt drove the Ottomans back to the coast; Sinan Pasha's reconquest took four years of fortress-by-fortress fighting and became a set-piece of Ottoman military literature.
nodes.src: al-Nahrawali, al-Barq al-Yamani; the Ottoman campaign accounts.

nodes.label: Forty years of mountain war
nodes.full: From al-Qasim's first rising to the Ottoman evacuation, the war ran for four decades of siege, ambush and shifting tribal allegiance. It ended not with a decisive battle but with the empire deciding Yemen cost more than it was worth.
nodes.src: Ghayat al-amani; the Ottoman decision to withdraw is discussed in Hathaway (2008).

nodes.label: Civil war and the loss of the coast
nodes.full: Rival imams, breakaway emirs, tribal war and then the Wahhabi and Egyptian invasions kept the highlands in near-continuous conflict for over a century, with the Tihama changing hands repeatedly.
nodes.src: Wilson's Gazetteer; al-Jirafi, al-Muqtataf min taʾrikh al-Yaman.

nodes.label: Taking and holding Aden
nodes.full: The 1839 landing was followed by repeated ʿAbdali and Fadli attempts to retake the port, all beaten off. Britain fortified the peninsula heavily and gradually pushed its treaty influence into the surrounding hills.
nodes.src: Waterfield, 'Sultans of Aden' (1968); Gavin (1975).

nodes.label: The highland insurgency that never ended
nodes.full: Ahmed Muhtar Pasha's reconquest was never completed. The 1891–92 rising under Imam al-Mansur nearly expelled the Ottomans again, and the war simmered on to 1900 and beyond, at a cost the empire could barely bear.
nodes.src: Farah, 'The Sultan's Yemen' (2002); Kuehn (2011).

nodes.label: The Ottoman coffee monopoly and the Mocha customs
nodes.full: The Ottomans tried to channel all coffee exports through a state monopoly and the Mocha customs house, and farmed the tobacco trade besides. The revenue was real but the burden — and the resented monopoly — fed the revolts that expelled them.
nodes.src: Michel Tuchscherer, 'Le commerce du café avant l'ère des plantations coloniales' (2001); Ottoman fiscal records for Yemen.

nodes.label: A Zaydi imamate governing Sunnis
nodes.full: For the first time the Zaydi imamate ruled a large majority-Shafiʿi population in the south and the Tihama. The Qasimids developed a pragmatic provincial administration and tax system for subjects who did not share their creed.
nodes.src: Haykel, 'Revival and Reform in Islam' (2003); Brinkley Messick, 'The Calligraphic State' (1993), on Yemeni legal administration.

nodes.label: The traditionist turn in Zaydi law
nodes.full: Qasimid imams appointed Ibn al-Amir al-Sanʿani and then al-Shawkani as chief judges and backed their argument for direct ijtihad from the hadith over loyalty to the Zaydi school — a state-sponsored move of Zaydi law toward Sunni traditionism.
nodes.src: Haykel, 'Revival and Reform in Islam' (2003).

nodes.label: The free port and the treaty system
nodes.full: Aden was declared a free port, run under Indian law from Bombay, and surrounded by a growing set of protection treaties that paid the hinterland chiefs a stipend in exchange for exclusive relations with Britain — the legal skeleton of the future Aden Protectorate.
nodes.src: Aitchison, 'A Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads'; Gavin (1975).

nodes.label: Zaydism as the creed of a state
nodes.full: Under the Qasimids, Zaydism was for the first time the official religion of a large territorial monarchy rather than the doctrine of a besieged mountain imamate. Ruling required compromises — hereditary succession, taxing non-believers — that strained the tradition.
nodes.src: Haykel (2003); vom Bruck, 'Islam, Memory, and Morality in Yemen' (2005).

nodes.label: Ibn al-Amir al-Sanʿani and al-Shawkani
nodes.full: Two Sanʿaʾ scholars attacked taqlid — following a school without re-examining its proofs — and insisted on returning directly to the Qurʾan and hadith. Both are now claimed as forerunners of the modern Salafi movement, though they worked from inside the Zaydi world.
nodes.src: Haykel, 'Revival and Reform in Islam' (2003); al-Shawkani's own al-Badr al-taliʿ.

nodes.label: Shrine and festival religion
nodes.full: The Tihama's Sufi lodges, the mawlid festivals at the great shrines, and the ʿAydarus cult at Aden carried the devotional life of ordinary Yemenis through the whole period, sometimes tolerated and sometimes attacked by the traditionist scholars.
nodes.src: al-Hibshi, 'al-Sufiyya wa'l-fuqahaʾ fi'l-Yaman'; ʿAbd Allah al-Hibshi on Yemeni Sufism.

nodes.label: Hadramawt turns outward
nodes.full: The ʿAlawi scholars of Tarim intensified their Indian Ocean mission — East Africa, the Hijaz, the Malabar coast and increasingly the Malay world — exporting a Shafiʿi-Sufi Islam and a family network that reached from Zanzibar to Singapore.
nodes.src: Engseng Ho, 'The Graves of Tarim' (2006); Ulrike Freitag, 'Indian Ocean Migrants and State Formation in Hadhramaut' (2003).

nodes.label: Wahhabi doctrine reaches the south
nodes.full: The first Saudi state carried Wahhabi preaching and raiders into Asir and Najran, sacking shrines and confronting both Zaydis and Sufis. The Yemeni argument over the doctrine — with al-Shawkani's followers partly sympathetic — began here.
nodes.src: the Saudi chronicles (Ibn Bishr) on the Asir campaigns; Haykel (2003) on the Yemeni reception.

nodes.label: The tower house and old Sanʿaʾ
nodes.full: Sanʿaʾ's houses rise five to nine storeys in stone and fired brick, their upper rooms lit by fanlights of coloured glass set in gypsum tracery. The walled old city, largely of this and earlier periods, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
nodes.src: Serjeant and Lewcock (eds), 'Sanʿaʾ: An Arabian Islamic City' (1983); Trevor Marchand, 'Minaret Building and Apprenticeship in Yemen' (2001).

nodes.label: Ottoman building in Yemen
nodes.full: The al-Bakiriyya mosque in Sanʿaʾ (1597), with its single great dome, brought the Ottoman central-plan mosque to Yemen; the second occupation added barracks, konaks and the port buildings of Hodeida. An imperial style sat awkwardly on local forms.
nodes.src: the al-Bakiriyya mosque; Nancy Um, 'The Merchant Houses of Mocha' (2009), on Ottoman-era architecture.

nodes.label: Mocha, the coffee port
nodes.full: At its height Mocha was a wall of tall merchant mansions, warehouses and the domed Shadhili mosque facing a road full of European ships. Within a century of losing the coffee trade it was a near-empty ruin on a silting bay.
nodes.src: Nancy Um, 'The Merchant Houses of Mocha: Trade and Architecture in an Indian Ocean Port' (2009).

nodes.label: Silver, the janbiya and the belt
nodes.full: Filigree and granulated silver jewellery — most of it made by Jewish silversmiths — and the curved janbiya dagger with its worked hilt and embroidered belt were the visible currency of rank and lineage in highland society.
nodes.src: Marjorie Transfeldt / Ester Muchawsky-Schnapper, 'The Jews of Yemen: Highlights of the Israel Museum Collection' (1994); Steven Caton on the janbiya.

nodes.label: The classical Sanʿani song
nodes.full: The ghinaʾ Sanʿani — colloquial humayni verse and classical qasida sung to the qanbus lute and copper tray — reached its recognised classical form in this period, performed at the afternoon qat gathering, the magyal.
nodes.src: Jean Lambert, 'La médecine de l'âme: le chant de Sanaa dans la société yéménite' (1997); Muhammad ʿAbduh Ghanim on the Sanʿani song.

nodes.label: Al-Shawkani's legal corpus
nodes.full: As chief judge of the Qasimid state for nearly forty years, al-Shawkani produced a huge traditionist output — Nayl al-awtar on hadith-based law, al-Sayl al-jarrar, the biographical dictionary al-Badr al-taliʿ — that shaped Islamic reform movements far beyond Yemen.
nodes.src: Haykel, 'Revival and Reform in Islam: The Legacy of Muhammad al-Shawkani' (2003).

nodes.label: The Yemeni chronicle tradition
nodes.full: Qasimid-era historians — Yahya ibn al-Husayn with Ghayat al-amani, Lutf Allah Jahhaf, later al-Wasiʿi and al-Jirafi — kept up a continuous, detailed local historiography that is the backbone of the modern history of the period.
nodes.src: Yahya ibn al-Husayn, Ghayat al-amani fi akhbar al-qutr al-Yamani; ʿAbd Allah al-Hibshi, 'Maṣadir al-fikr al-ʿArabi al-Islami fi al-Yaman'.

nodes.label: The Niebuhr expedition
nodes.full: A Danish royal expedition of six reached Yemen to study its geography, plants, languages and antiquities. Five members died of disease; the surveyor Carsten Niebuhr survived to publish the first accurate European maps and description of the country.
nodes.src: Carsten Niebuhr, 'Beschreibung von Arabien' (1772) and 'Reisebeschreibung nach Arabien' (1774–78); Thorkild Hansen, 'Arabia Felix' (1962).

nodes.label: Coffee botany and the broken monopoly
nodes.full: European merchants and naturalists studied the coffee shrub at Mocha and then propagated it: the Dutch to Java and Amsterdam, the French to Réunion. The plant that Yemen had guarded for a century was cultivable anywhere warm enough.
nodes.src: William Ukers, 'All About Coffee' (1922); Tuchscherer (2001) on the plant's transfer.

nodes.label: Mocha and the world coffee monopoly
nodes.full: For roughly a century Yemen was the only source of coffee for the world market. Dutch, English and French factories at Mocha competed for the crop, and the customs revenue underwrote the Qasimid state.
nodes.src: Tuchscherer, 'Le commerce du café' (2001); Um, 'The Merchant Houses of Mocha' (2009).

nodes.label: The monopoly broken, Mocha declines
nodes.full: Once coffee grew in Java, Réunion, the Caribbean and Brazil, Yemen's share of the market collapsed within a generation. Mocha's trade drained away through the 18th and 19th centuries and the port silted into insignificance.
nodes.src: Tuchscherer (2001); the fall in Mocha's shipping is documented in the East India Company factory records.

nodes.label: Aden reborn as a coaling port
nodes.full: From a village of a few hundred people in 1839, Aden grew — especially after Suez in 1869 — into one of the world's busiest bunkering ports, its coal, water and provisions serving the steamer traffic between Europe and Asia. Almost none of that touched the interior.
nodes.src: Gavin, 'Aden under British Rule' (1975); the Aden port statistics in the Bombay administration reports.

nodes.label: The highlands turn inward
nodes.full: Cut off from the collapsed coast trade, the highlands ran a near-subsistence economy of terraced grain, and qat spread onto land that had grown coffee and cereals — a stimulant crop for a market that was now purely local.
nodes.src: Shelagh Weir, 'Qat in Yemen: Consumption and Social Change' (2007); Varisco on highland land use.

nodes.label: The Red Sea slave trade and its suppression
nodes.full: Enslaved people from the Horn of Africa and the East African coast were shipped through the Yemeni ports throughout the period. The British at Aden, and later the Ottomans, moved against the traffic from the mid-19th century, with slow and partial effect.
nodes.src: the anti-slavery correspondence in the Aden Residency records; William Gervase Clarence-Smith, 'Islam and the Abolition of Slavery' (2006).

nodes.label: The Ottoman fortress network
nodes.full: Both Ottoman occupations rested on a chain of star forts and blockhouses commanding the passes and the towns. Holding Yemen was an engineering problem as much as a military one, and the forts outlasted the garrisons.
nodes.src: the Ottoman military engineering records for Yemen; Kuehn (2011) on the garrison system.

nodes.label: Steam, cable and condenser at Aden
nodes.full: Aden became a node of the imperial grid: a submarine telegraph cable from 1870, coal depots and workshops, and steam condensers that made drinking water from the sea — technology that connected the port to London and Bombay while the interior had none of it.
nodes.src: Gavin (1975); the Eastern Telegraph Company records; the Aden condenser plant.

nodes.label: Keeping the terraces alive
nodes.full: Through political collapse and economic isolation, highland communities went on maintaining terrace walls, spate channels and cisterns generation after generation — the undramatic engineering that let an inward-turned country feed itself.
nodes.src: Tony Wilkinson and Christopher Edens on Yemeni terrace systems; Varisco (1994).

nodes.label: Yemen and the Ottoman Empire
nodes.full: The Ottomans held Yemen for the Red Sea and the prestige of guarding the pilgrimage — a distant, loss-making, chronically rebellious province they occupied twice and never fully controlled.
nodes.src: Hathaway, 'The Arab Lands under Ottoman Rule' (2008); Farah, 'The Sultan's Yemen' (2002).

nodes.label: The European companies at Mocha
nodes.full: The Dutch VOC, the English East India Company and the French Compagnie des Indes all kept factories at Mocha to buy coffee. Their competition set the world price, and their meticulous records are a main source for the whole period.
nodes.src: Um, 'The Merchant Houses of Mocha' (2009); the VOC and EIC Mocha factory archives.

nodes.label: Aden as a piece of British India
nodes.full: Aden was governed from Bombay, defended by the Indian Army, provisioned and populated from the subcontinent, and administered under Indian law. On the Arabian coast it functioned as an outpost of British India, not of Britain.
nodes.src: Gavin, 'Aden under British Rule' (1975); Scott Reese, 'Imperial Muslims: Islam, Community and Authority in the Indian Ocean, 1839–1937' (2018).

nodes.label: The Hadrami diaspora matures
nodes.full: By 1900 Hadrami communities were long established across the Indian Ocean, from the Nizam's armies in Hyderabad to the merchant houses of Singapore and Java. Their remittances kept the Kathiri and Quʿayti sultanates of Hadramawt solvent.
nodes.src: Ulrike Freitag, 'Indian Ocean Migrants and State Formation in Hadhramaut' (2003); Ho, 'The Graves of Tarim' (2006).

nodes.label: The undrawn Anglo-Ottoman line
nodes.full: From the 1870s Britain at Aden and the Ottomans in the highlands faced each other across an undefined frontier, each claiming the tribes in between. The joint boundary commission that finally drew the 'violet line' was convened only at the very end of the century.
nodes.src: the Anglo-Ottoman boundary papers, 1902–05; Gavin (1975).

nodes.label: The one unified Zaydi Yemen
nodes.full: For a few decades in the 17th century a single native dynasty ruled the whole of Yemen from the highlands to the sea. It is a high-water mark of Yemeni self-rule that was not reached again until the unification of 1990.
nodes.src: Dresch, 'A History of Modern Yemen' (2000); the Qasimid chronicles.

nodes.label: From coffee monopoly to backwater
nodes.full: Losing the coffee monopoly took away Yemen's one world-scale asset. What followed was a long slide into economic marginality on the edge of whichever empire happened to be present — Ottoman, Egyptian, British.
nodes.src: Tuchscherer (2001); Dresch (2000).

nodes.label: The steamship cuts the country in two
nodes.full: Suez made Aden a global port wired to London and Bombay while the highlands turned further inward. The modern gulf between a coast plugged into the world economy and a subsistence interior opens here.
nodes.src: Gavin (1975); Dresch (2000).

nodes.label: The thread continues — three Yemens in 1900
nodes.full: By 1900 Yemen was British at Aden, Ottoman on the coast and around Sanʿaʾ, and effectively autonomous under the Hamid al-Din imams in the Zaydi highlands. That three-way split is the situation the 20th century — and the next folio — inherits.
nodes.src: a forward reference: yemen-1900-today (Imam Yahya's kingdom, the two republics, unification, and the current war) is planned but not yet built.

nodes.label: The Mawzaʿ Exile
nodes.full: Imam al-Mahdi Ahmad ordered almost the entire Jewish population expelled to the fierce heat of the coast at Mawzaʿ. Many died; the survivors were recalled a year later to fewer rights, banned from the walled cities, and it became the defining trauma of Yemeni Jewry.
nodes.src: the Jewish accounts collected by Yosef Qafih and others; Yosef Tobi, 'The Jews of Yemen' (1999).

nodes.label: The Jewish craft economy and Shalom Shabazi
nodes.full: Barred from land and many trades, Yemeni Jews concentrated in silverwork, ironwork, weaving and other crafts, and produced in the 17th-century poet Shalom Shabazi a devotional tradition sung to this day. They lived under the dhimma across every dynasty.
nodes.src: Tobi, 'The Jews of Yemen' (1999); Yosef Tobi and others on Shabazi's diwan.

nodes.label: The Akhdam of the Tihama
nodes.full: A hereditary group confined to menial work and to settlements at the edge of Tihama towns, the Akhdam ('servants') sat below even the ordinary poor. Their origin was explained by contested myths tying them to the pre-Islamic Ethiopian presence.
nodes.src: Delores Walters and Huda Seif on the Akhdam / muhamashin; Gabriele vom Bruck on Yemeni status hierarchy.

nodes.label: Enslaved Africans in Yemen
nodes.full: Domestic and military slavery, fed by the Red Sea trade from the Horn and East Africa, was a normal part of elite and state life. Abolition came late and from outside — British pressure at Aden from mid-century — and lingered in the highlands into the 20th.
nodes.src: Clarence-Smith, 'Islam and the Abolition of Slavery' (2006); the Aden Residency anti-slavery files.
